title: Welcome to the DDS Marine Blog
author: Capt. Dinesh
excerpt: Introducing the DDS Marine blog — your source for insights on marine operations, STS transfers, and the maritime industry in Malaysia and beyond.
content:
Welcome to the DDS Marine Energy Services blog! We're excited to launch this platform to share industry insights, company updates, and technical knowledge about the maritime world.

At DDS Marine, we specialize in Ship-to-Ship (STS) transfers, deep-draft pilotage, mooring master services, bunkering, chartering, and marine advisory. Based in Penang and operating across the Straits of Malacca, our team brings decades of experience to every operation.

Through this blog, we'll cover topics like:

  • STS operations best practices
  • Marine safety and regulations
  • Industry trends in Malaysian waters
  • Company milestones and project highlights
  • Technical insights from our team

Stay tuned for regular updates. If you have questions or topics you'd like us to cover, get in touch!

title: Successful Cargo Discharge & Loading at FOTT Terminal
author: Capt. Dinesh
excerpt: DDS Marine successfully completed cargo discharge and loading operations at FOTT Terminal — a testament to meticulous planning, seamless coordination, and crew dedication.
content:
We are proud to share the successful cargo discharge and loading operations at FOTT Terminal, executed safely and efficiently by our team onboard our Panamax tanker.

Every successful port call is the result of meticulous planning, seamless coordination, and the dedication of our vessel crew, terminal personnel, surveyors, agents, and all stakeholders involved.

At DDS Marine Energy Services, we remain committed to delivering safe, reliable, and efficient marine transportation while maintaining the highest operational and safety standards.

A sincere thank you to everyone who contributed to another smooth and successful operation. Here's to many more successful voyages ahead.

title: DDS Marine Supports Marine Salvage Operation
author: Capt. Dinesh
excerpt: DDS Marine provided marine and operational support during the salvage and recovery of M/V HUGE KUMANO following its collision with M/V CAPE XL in the Singapore Strait.
content:
DDS Marine Energy Services Sdn Bhd is proud to have provided marine and operational support in connection with the salvage and recovery operation of M/V HUGE KUMANO (IMO 9889277) following the vessel's collision in the Singapore Strait.

On 20 May 2026, the Panama-flagged Capesize bulk carrier HUGE KUMANO was involved in a collision with M/V CAPE XL, resulting in significant structural damage to the port side of the vessel.

Vessel Particulars – M/V HUGE KUMANO

  • IMO: 9889277
  • Type: Capesize Bulk Carrier
  • Flag: Panama
  • Year Built: 2020
  • LOA: Approx. 300 metres
  • Beam: 50 metres
  • Deadweight: Approx. 208,848 MT

Following the casualty, DDS Marine was engaged in supporting the marine operation, working alongside the relevant parties and marine teams to facilitate the safe execution of the required recovery and operational activities.

Operations of this nature demand careful coordination, experienced marine personnel and, above all, an uncompromising commitment to safety.

We are pleased to have contributed our marine expertise and operational resources toward the successful handling of this challenging casualty operation.

Safety. Experience. Operational Readiness.

title: Strait of Hormuz: Iran Reports Supertanker Mine Strike
author: DDS Marine Intelligence Desk
excerpt: Iran's IRGC Navy says a supertanker carrying over two million barrels of crude exploded after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz. What we know, what remains unverified, and what it means for tanker operators.
content:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on 17 October 2026 that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz. It is the latest in a run of mine incidents the IRGC has reported this month, and it adds to the risk picture for every owner, charterer and operator with exposure to Gulf liftings.

What was reported

According to the IRGC statement, carried by Iranian state media including IRNA and Tasnim, the tanker was attempting to transit the strait on a route Iran has not authorised. The IRGC said the vessel had switched off its positioning and radar systems to avoid detection, and claimed it was operating with US military support. Some reports of the statement say the blast hit the engine room and left the tanker without propulsion.

The IRGC did not name the vessel or give its flag, ownership, crew status or exact position. Images released alongside the statement have not been independently verified, and at the time of writing no owner, flag state or maritime security centre has publicly confirmed the incident.

Part of a wider pattern this month

The 17 October claim follows several similar statements in quick succession:

  • 12 October: the IRGC said a supertanker of around two million barrels' capacity hit a mine with its navigation systems switched off, describing it as the third vessel to strike mines on the "prohibited route" in a matter of days.
  • 14 October: the IRGC said a container ship sank after hitting a mine. Separately, UKMTO received a report of a container ship struck by an unidentified projectile near the exit of the strait.
  • 17 October: some outlets reported the latest tanker as the second such incident within hours.

These incidents sit against months of disruption. Iran announced in July that it had again closed the strait, and while US Central Command said in late August that shipping lanes had reopened after mine clearance, Iran has continued to insist that vessels follow its own routing rules. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War have also suggested that vessels conducting ship-to-ship transfers in and around the strait may be a particular focus.

What remains unclear

Every detail of the 17 October incident currently rests on a single source: the IRGC itself. Without a vessel name, IMO number or independent imagery, it is not yet possible to confirm the scale of damage, the condition of the crew, or whether any cargo has been released. DDS Marine will update its assessment as flag states, owners, UKMTO or the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) publish further information.

DDS view: what it means for the market

War-risk costs are likely to stay high. Repeated reports of mine strikes, verified or not, tend to keep additional war-risk premiums for Gulf calls elevated and can narrow the pool of owners willing to fix for Arabian Gulf loadings.

Dark transits carry new risk. The IRGC has repeatedly linked these incidents to vessels sailing with AIS switched off. Owners should weigh that carefully against their own security advice, since the practice may draw scrutiny from more than one direction.

Knock-on effects reach Asia. Much of the crude moving through Hormuz is bound for Asian refiners. Disruption at the strait can lengthen voyages, shift cargo flows and increase demand for storage and ship-to-ship capacity in hubs along the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Operators in our region should plan for that volatility.

Practical steps for owners and charterers

  • Follow the latest UKMTO and JMIC advisories before and during any Gulf transit.
  • Review war-risk cover, listed-area status and additional premium terms with brokers and underwriters before fixing.
  • Check charter party war-risk and Hormuz-specific clauses, including rights to refuse orders and how added costs are allocated.
  • Brief masters and crews on mine awareness, reporting lines and emergency procedures.
  • Build realistic schedule buffers for Asia-bound cargoes, including possible delays at loading and transfer points.

Outlook

Until the facts of the latest incident are independently confirmed, the market is likely to keep pricing in risk rather than waiting for certainty. DDS Marine continues to monitor developments in the Strait of Hormuz and their effect on tanker operations across Southeast Asia, and covers them each week in the DDS Weekly Maritime Intelligence. For operational support with STS transfers, chartering or marine assurance, contact our team.

Sources: IRGC Navy statement as reported by Bernama/IRNA, RFE/RL and Shafaq News; earlier incidents from Bernama/Anadolu and Ahram Online. Details have not been independently verified.
